title: Coricidin and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Drowsiness, DXM, and Liver Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on Coricidin HBP? How chlorpheniramine, dextromethorphan, and acetaminophen interact with alcohol, how long to wait, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Coricidin HBP? How its antihistamine, DXM, and acetaminophen interact with alcohol, how long to wait, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** you shouldn't drink alcohol while taking Coricidin. Every Coricidin HBP label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks, and the reason is simple. Most Coricidin products contain **chlorpheniramine**, a sedating antihistamine, and many also contain **dextromethorphan (DXM)**, a cough suppressant that acts on the brain. Both slow you down, and alcohol slows you down too. Stack all three and you can end up far drowsier, dizzier, and more impaired than any one of them would make you on its own. Some Coricidin versions also contain **acetaminophen**, which brings the same liver concerns as Tylenol and alcohol.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink while you have Coricidin in your system. If you already took a dose and then had a drink or two, don't take another dose that night, don't drive, and stay with someone if you feel unusually sleepy or unsteady. Read the Drug Facts box on your exact box, because the Coricidin lineup includes several different formulas. If you think you or someone else took more than the label allows, or mixed it with a lot of alcohol, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away. In an emergency, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Coricidin with alcohol, and especially if** you take an antidepressant (SSRIs, SNRIs, or MAO inhibitors), sleep medicine, anxiety medicine, opioid painkillers, or other cold products; you have liver disease or drink heavily on a regular basis; or you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or breathing problems. **Get emergency help (911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222)** if someone is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly, has a seizure, has a racing heart with fever and muscle twitching, or is confused or seeing things that aren't there.

## What Is Coricidin HBP, and Why Is It Different?

Coricidin HBP is a line of over-the-counter cold, cough, and flu medicines made by Bayer. The "HBP" stands for high blood pressure. The selling point is what it leaves out: Coricidin HBP products don't contain a nasal decongestant like pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine. Decongestants can raise blood pressure and heart rate, so Coricidin is often the product pharmacists point people with high blood pressure toward.

That's a real benefit, but it's worth being clear about what it means for drinking. "Safe for high blood pressure" refers to the missing decongestant. It says nothing about alcohol. The ingredients Coricidin *does* contain are the ones that interact with alcohol most directly.

Depending on the version, a Coricidin HBP product may contain some combination of:

- **Chlorpheniramine maleate**, a first-generation antihistamine for runny nose and sneezing. It causes drowsiness.
- **Dextromethorphan HBr (DXM)**, a cough suppressant that works in the brain.
- **Acetaminophen**, a pain and fever reliever (the drug in Tylenol).
- **Guaifenesin**, an expectorant that thins mucus (the drug in Mucinex).

The exact mix and strength depend on which box you bought. Product names like "Cold & Flu," "Cough & Cold," "Maximum Strength Flu," "Chest Congestion & Cough," and nighttime versions each use a different formula, and manufacturers update formulas over time. So the first step is always the same: turn the box over and read the active ingredients in the Drug Facts panel. Below, we go through what each ingredient does when alcohol is added.

## How Coricidin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

The main problem is that Coricidin and alcohol push on the same system. Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant, which means it slows down brain activity. It makes you relaxed and sleepy at low doses, and it slows your reactions, coordination, judgment, and eventually breathing at higher doses. Two of Coricidin's main ingredients have overlapping effects.

### Chlorpheniramine plus alcohol: extra drowsiness

Chlorpheniramine is an older antihistamine, from the same family as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and doxylamine (the sleep ingredient in NyQuil). These older antihistamines cross into the brain easily and block histamine there. Histamine in the brain helps keep you awake and alert, so blocking it makes you sleepy. That's why newer antihistamines like loratadine (Claritin) and cetirizine (Zyrtec) were designed to stay mostly out of the brain.

When you add alcohol, the sedation adds up. You feel the drowsiness of the antihistamine plus the drowsiness of the alcohol, and the combination can feel stronger than you'd expect from either one. In practice, that means slower reaction times, poorer coordination, and a higher chance of falls or accidents. It's the reason every label for a product with chlorpheniramine says that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness, and to be careful driving or operating machinery.

Chlorpheniramine also has **anticholinergic** effects, meaning it blocks a chemical messenger (acetylcholine) that controls things like saliva, bladder emptying, and focusing your eyes. That's what causes the dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, and trouble urinating some people get. Alcohol already dehydrates you and dries out your mouth, so the two together can leave you feeling parched and foggy. In older adults, anticholinergic medicines are linked to confusion, and alcohol makes that more likely.

### Dextromethorphan plus alcohol: dizziness and impairment

DXM is the "DM" in many cough syrups. At the dose on the label, it calms the cough reflex in the brain. It's generally considered safe when used as directed. But it does affect the brain, and its common side effects include dizziness, drowsiness, and nausea. Alcohol makes all three more likely.

DXM also has a quirk that matters if you take other medicines. It's broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP2D6**, and it affects serotonin, a brain chemical tied to mood. That's why DXM labels warn against taking it with MAO inhibitors (an older class of antidepressants) and why pharmacists are careful about combining it with SSRIs and SNRIs, such as fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), or paroxetine (Paxil). In rare cases, the combination can contribute to **serotonin syndrome**, a reaction caused by too much serotonin activity. Some of these antidepressants also slow down CYP2D6, so DXM can build up to higher levels than usual. Alcohol isn't the direct cause of serotonin syndrome, but it can blur the early warning signs and make the dizziness and confusion worse.

Taking more than the labeled dose of DXM is dangerous, especially with alcohol and especially with products that also contain chlorpheniramine, because the antihistamine dose climbs too. If anyone has taken more than the label says, treat it as a poisoning risk and call Poison Control.

### Acetaminophen plus alcohol: the liver question

Some Coricidin products, particularly the "Cold & Flu" and "Flu" versions, contain acetaminophen. That brings in a separate concern, which is the liver. A small share of every acetaminophen dose gets turned into a toxic by-product that the liver has to neutralize. Regular heavy drinking makes the liver produce more of that by-product and lowers its ability to clean it up. That's why the FDA-required label on acetaminophen products warns that severe liver damage may occur if you have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using it.

The bigger practical danger is doubling up without realizing it. If you take a Coricidin product with acetaminophen and then take Tylenol for a hangover headache, you can go over the daily limit faster than you'd think. We cover this in detail in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

### Guaifenesin plus alcohol: the mildest part

Guaifenesin, the expectorant in "Chest Congestion" versions, doesn't have a strong direct interaction with alcohol. It can cause some dizziness or nausea on its own, and alcohol can make those a bit worse. The bigger issues come from whatever else is in the same box. Our [Mucinex and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/mucinex-and-alcohol) covers guaifenesin on its own.

## Ingredient-by-Ingredient Summary

| Ingredient | What it does | What alcohol adds | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorpheniramine | Dries up runny nose and sneezing | More drowsiness, dry mouth, foggy thinking | Sedation, falls, impaired driving |
| Dextromethorphan (DXM) | Suppresses cough | More dizziness, drowsiness, nausea | Impairment; serotonin interactions with some antidepressants |
| Acetaminophen | Relieves pain and fever | Extra load on the liver | Liver damage with heavy drinking or too much acetaminophen |
| Guaifenesin | Thins mucus | Mild extra dizziness or nausea | Low on its own |

## I Already Drank. Can I Take Coricidin?

This is one of the most common versions of the question: you had a few drinks, now you're sniffly or coughing, and you want to take something before bed.

The safest answer is to wait. Coricidin's ingredients and alcohol both cause drowsiness, and combining them right before sleep can make you sleep more heavily than usual and wake up groggier. That's not just unpleasant. Heavy sedation on top of alcohol can make it harder to wake up if you're sick in the night, and it raises the risk of falls if you get up in the dark.

Some general pointers, not personal advice:

- **After one or two drinks**, a healthy adult's body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. Waiting until the alcohol has worn off before taking a dose is a reasonable approach. If you're not sure, skip the dose tonight.
- **After a heavy night**, don't take Coricidin until the next day, once you've slept, eaten, and feel sober.
- **If your version contains acetaminophen**, count it toward your daily total and don't add Tylenol or another product that also contains it.
- **Don't take a second cold medicine "to be sure."** Many cold and flu products share the same ingredients. Doubling up is one of the most common ways people end up taking too much.

If you just need relief from a runny nose while you wait, plain saline nasal spray, a humidifier, warm fluids, and honey for a cough (for adults and children over one year old) are all ways to feel better without adding a sedative.

## I Took Coricidin. How Long Should I Wait Before Drinking?

There's no official waiting period printed on the box. The label simply says to avoid alcoholic drinks while using the product. If you're taking Coricidin every 4 to 6 hours for a cold, you're "using the product" the whole time you're dosing, so the honest answer is that it's best to skip alcohol until you've stopped taking it.

If you took a single dose earlier in the day and want to know when it's reasonably out of your system, keep in mind that chlorpheniramine sticks around longer than most people expect. It has a long half-life, often reported in the range of roughly a day in adults, which means its effects can last well beyond the 4 to 6 hours between doses. DXM's effects usually wear off sooner, but people break it down at very different speeds because of genetic differences in the CYP2D6 enzyme. So "it's been six hours" doesn't guarantee the drowsiness is gone.

A practical way to think about it: if you still feel any drowsiness, dry mouth, or slowness from the medicine, it's still active, and alcohol will add to it. Waiting until the next day after your last dose is a sensible margin for most people. If you have a specific event coming up and you're sick, it's worth asking a pharmacist which product (if any) fits your plans.

## Coricidin Cough & Cold and Alcohol

The "Cough & Cold" version is the one most people mean when they search this question. It pairs **DXM** with **chlorpheniramine**, so it combines both of the ingredients that interact most with alcohol: the cough suppressant that can cause dizziness and the antihistamine that causes drowsiness. Of the Coricidin products, this pairing has the most direct overlap with alcohol's effects on the brain.

If you're using this version, the main things to avoid are drinking while you're dosing, driving after taking it (with or without alcohol, until you know how it affects you), and combining it with other sedating products such as sleep aids, NyQuil, Benadryl, or anxiety medicines. Also check for interactions with antidepressants, because of the DXM.

## Coricidin Cold & Flu and Alcohol

"Cold & Flu" versions typically pair **chlorpheniramine** with **acetaminophen**. That means two separate concerns at once: the extra drowsiness from the antihistamine, and the liver load from acetaminophen. The "Maximum Strength Flu" version can include all three (acetaminophen, chlorpheniramine, and DXM), so it carries every risk on this page.

With these versions, keep a careful count of acetaminophen. The general daily upper limit for healthy adults is 4,000 mg, and the label tells people who have 3 or more drinks every day to ask a doctor before use. If you're likely to wake up with a headache after drinking, don't reach for Tylenol on top of a Coricidin flu product. Our guide to [cough medicine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) also lists other common cold products that contain hidden acetaminophen.

## Coricidin vs. NyQuil, DayQuil, and Other Cold Medicines With Alcohol

It helps to see Coricidin next to the other products people reach for, because the interaction with alcohol depends on what's inside, not the brand name.

- **NyQuil** usually combines acetaminophen, DXM, and doxylamine, another sedating antihistamine. Some liquid versions have historically contained alcohol as an ingredient themselves. The alcohol interaction is similar to Coricidin's: heavy drowsiness plus liver load. See our [NyQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol).
- **DayQuil** usually combines acetaminophen, DXM, and phenylephrine (a decongestant) but no sedating antihistamine. It tends to be less sedating than Coricidin, but it isn't suitable for people avoiding decongestants. See [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol).
- **Benadryl** (diphenhydramine) is in the same antihistamine family as chlorpheniramine and is, if anything, more sedating. See [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover).
- **Newer antihistamines** like loratadine and cetirizine cause less drowsiness, although their labels still advise caution with alcohol. See [Claritin and alcohol](/never-hungover/claritin-and-alcohol) and [Zyrtec and alcohol](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol).

The common thread is that the sedating antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, doxylamine) and DXM are the ingredients to watch with alcohol. If you'd like a list of options that don't contain alcohol as an ingredient, our [alcohol-free cold medicine guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) has one.

## Does Coricidin Contain Alcohol?

Coricidin HBP tablets and capsules aren't liquids, so alcohol isn't a typical part of their formula the way it historically was in some cough syrups. Still, inactive ingredients vary by product and change over time, so if you need to avoid alcohol completely (for example, for religious reasons or because you take a medicine that reacts badly with any alcohol), check the inactive ingredients list on your box or ask the pharmacist. Our post on [whether cough syrup has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-cough-syrup-have-alcohol) explains how to read those labels.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Coricidin and alcohol if you:

- **Take an antidepressant**, especially an MAO inhibitor (which DXM labels say not to combine with at all, including within two weeks of stopping one) or an SSRI or SNRI. Ask a pharmacist before taking any DXM product.
- **Take other sedating medicines**, such as sleep aids, benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), opioid painkillers, muscle relaxers, gabapentin, or certain seizure medicines. Combining several sedatives with alcohol can dangerously slow breathing.
- **Are an older adult.** Sedating, anticholinergic antihistamines are linked to confusion and falls in older people, and many experts advise older adults to avoid them where possible. Alcohol adds to both risks.
- **Have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or trouble urinating.** Chlorpheniramine's label tells people with these conditions to ask a doctor first.
- **Have breathing problems** like asthma, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis, which the label also lists.
- **Have liver disease or drink 3 or more drinks most days**, if your version contains acetaminophen.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Check with a doctor before using any cold medicine, and alcohol is best avoided in pregnancy in any case.

If any of these apply, a five-minute chat with a pharmacist is the best move. They can look at your full medication list and suggest a cold product that fits.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink while taking a normal dose of Coricidin will just feel more tired and foggy than usual. But some reactions need urgent care. Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if you notice any of the following in yourself or someone else:

- **Very hard to wake up**, or can't stay awake
- **Slow, shallow, or irregular breathing**
- **Severe confusion, agitation, or hallucinations** (seeing or hearing things that aren't there)
- **A seizure**
- **A racing heart, high fever, heavy sweating, shivering, muscle twitching or stiffness**, especially if the person takes an antidepressant (these can be signs of serotonin syndrome)
- **Very hot, flushed, dry skin with a fast heartbeat and inability to urinate** (signs of too much antihistamine)
- **Vomiting and feeling very unwell the next day** after a product with acetaminophen, or pain under the right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine

If someone is very drowsy after mixing medicine and alcohol, don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." Lay them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and get help. Poison Control is free, confidential, and open around the clock, and they'd much rather hear from you early.

## Safer Ways to Handle a Cold and a Night Out

If you're sick and have plans that involve drinking, the most honest advice is to skip the drinks this time. Alcohol doesn't help a cold, it can disrupt the sleep your body needs to recover, and it dehydrates you at a time when you need fluids. Our article on [whether alcohol helps a cold](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold) explains why the "hot toddy cures a cold" idea doesn't hold up.

If you do decide to go out:

- **Don't take Coricidin before or during the evening.** Choose between the medicine and the drinks.
- **Use non-drug relief while you're out**, such as throat lozenges, water between drinks, and saline spray before you leave.
- **Keep it to one or two drinks**, eat a real meal first, and drink water alongside.
- **Take your next dose the following day**, after you've slept and eaten, and only if you still need it.
- **Don't drive** if you've had any alcohol and any sedating medicine in the same day.

For a broader look at which everyday medicines clash with alcohol, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Because this is a hangover-focused site, we'll be clear about what supplements can and can't do here. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven.

DHM does **not** make it safe to combine Coricidin with alcohol. There is no good evidence that it reduces the drowsiness from antihistamines, changes how DXM behaves, or protects the liver from acetaminophen. Its interactions with cold medicines haven't been well studied, so if you take prescription medicines, ask a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

Where DHM may fit is on ordinary nights out when you're *not* taking cold medicine. Some people use it alongside the basics (eating first, pacing drinks, and staying hydrated) that our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers. If you want to try it, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Coricidin HBP is built for people with high blood pressure because it skips the decongestant, but that has nothing to do with alcohol safety.
- Its main ingredients, **chlorpheniramine** and **DXM**, both slow the brain. Alcohol does too, and the effects add up to extra drowsiness, dizziness, and impairment.
- Versions with **acetaminophen** add a liver concern, especially for people who drink 3 or more drinks a day or who also take Tylenol.
- The label says to avoid alcohol while using the product. The safest plan is to skip drinks until you've finished your last dose and the drowsiness has worn off.
- Check with a pharmacist if you take antidepressants, sedatives, or other cold medicines, and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 for very heavy drowsiness, slow breathing, confusion, or signs of overdose.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Coricidin?**

It's best not to. Coricidin HBP labels say to avoid alcoholic drinks while using the product. Most versions contain chlorpheniramine, a sedating antihistamine, and many contain dextromethorphan (DXM). Both add to alcohol's effects on the brain, which can cause extra drowsiness, dizziness, and impaired coordination. Versions with acetaminophen also add a liver concern. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure about your specific product.

**How long after taking Coricidin can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. The label says to avoid alcohol while you're using the product, so the simplest approach is to skip drinks until you've stopped taking it. Chlorpheniramine can stay in your system for a long time (its half-life is often reported at around a day in adults), so waiting until the day after your last dose, and until any drowsiness is gone, is a sensible margin for most people.

**Can I take Coricidin after drinking?**

It's safer to wait until the alcohol has worn off. Taking a sedating cold medicine right after drinking can make you much drowsier than usual. After a heavy night, wait until the next day, after you've slept and eaten. If your version contains acetaminophen, count it toward your daily total and don't add Tylenol on top.

**Is Coricidin Cough and Cold safe with alcohol?**

No. Coricidin Cough & Cold combines dextromethorphan and chlorpheniramine, the two ingredients that overlap most with alcohol's effects. Together with alcohol, they can cause strong drowsiness, dizziness, and slowed reactions. Avoid drinking while you're taking it, don't drive, and check with a pharmacist if you take antidepressants or other sedating medicines.

**Is Coricidin Cold and Flu safe with alcohol?**

It's best avoided. Cold & Flu versions usually contain chlorpheniramine and acetaminophen, so alcohol adds both extra drowsiness and extra liver load. The acetaminophen label warns that people who have 3 or more drinks every day should ask a doctor before use. Never combine it with Tylenol or other acetaminophen products.

**Why is Coricidin called HBP, and does that make it safer with alcohol?**

HBP stands for high blood pressure. Coricidin HBP products leave out nasal decongestants, which can raise blood pressure. That makes them a common choice for people with hypertension, but it doesn't make them any safer with alcohol. The ingredients that interact with alcohol, chlorpheniramine and DXM, are still there.

**What happens if you mix Coricidin and alcohol by accident?**

If it was a normal dose and a drink or two, the most likely effect is feeling more tired, dizzy, or foggy than usual. Don't take another dose, don't drive, drink water, and have someone check on you. Get emergency help if someone is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly, is confused or hallucinating, has a seizure, or has a racing heart with fever and muscle twitching. Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) can advise you any time.

**Does DHM make it safe to take Coricidin with alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the drowsiness from antihistamines, changes how dextromethorphan works, or protects the liver from acetaminophen, and its interactions with cold medicines haven't been well studied. Follow the Coricidin label and avoid alcohol while using it, whatever supplements you take.
